title: Swiss inflation persistence and the forecasts a seasonal rule could match
summary: Simon Beyeler asks whether forecasters could have recognised a lasting component in the 2021–23 Swiss inflation surge while it was happening. Models fitted to headline CPI and to 22 categories both picked up persistence. In the sectoral model, much of the movement came from durable changes within individual categories.

Persistence and forecasting skill answer different questions. Table 1 compares forecasts of a three-month CPI change from 180 monthly starting dates in 2010–24. Three months ahead, the sectoral model cut root-mean-square error by 39% against repeating the latest observation. Repeating last year’s seasonal value cut it by 47.4% against the same benchmark.

questions.question: Why fit the trend recursively?
questions.detail: Later observations help distinguish a temporary jump from a lasting shift. Truncating the data at each forecast date tests what an analyst could plausibly have inferred then.

questions.question: What do the relative errors mean in inflation units?
questions.detail: At three months the benchmark error is 0.877 percentage points. Multiplying it by 0.610 gives about 0.535 points for the sectoral model. The seasonal rule’s ratio of 0.526 gives about 0.461 points.

questions.question: How would one test the model against that challenger?
questions.detail: Compare their paired errors at a prespecified horizon, allowing for overlapping observations, then repeat the exercise on new dates. Table 1 reports significance relative to the latest-observation benchmark.

limitation: This is staff research. The sample spans a particular inflation cycle and its forecast windows overlap. The model’s statistical trend cannot identify the economic shock responsible for a price rise.
